nl_marine_lab.blurb: A seaside bouldering wall at Logy Bay, a short drive from St. John's on the Avalon Peninsula. The face is steep red sandstone that sits right at the water, looking across a little inlet at the research building. Twelve boulder problems run from easy V0 up through the V4 to V7 range, with a couple of V10 and a far-off project grade at the top, so beginners and strong climbers both find something. A single short ice line forms here in winter. The walk from the car is only a few minutes, which makes it a handy after-work stop.
nl_marine_lab.parking_note: Leave the car in the East Coast Trail lot on Marine Lab Road, just before the research facility. From St. John's, follow Logy Bay Road, turn onto Marine Drive and bear right at the fork onto Marine Lab Road.
nl_marine_lab.approach: Take the trail from the lot toward the water, continue through a rocky stretch and round a corner; the steep wall appears across the inlet from the lab building. A few minutes on foot.

nl_after_work_wall.blurb: A compact sport crag near Corner Brook on Newfoundland's west side, nearest to the road of the crags in this pocket and often chosen for a quick session. Thirteen routes, almost all bolted, are steep and athletic on well-featured, overhanging rock, with a ledge cutting across the wall. Grades start near 5.9 and reach into the 5.12s, with the bulk between 5.10 and 5.12. Rock quality is mixed and loose holds turn up, so a helmet and care about where you stand are wise. There are no rappel stations; walk down the same way you came.
nl_after_work_wall.parking_note: Pull onto the road shoulder at the top of the hill just beyond the dump, a little past the sign warning of trucks entering.
nl_after_work_wall.approach: Follow the obvious trail from the roadside toward the cliffs. At the fork take the left branch, marked with orange flagging tape; it climbs steeply up the right side of a small valley and is faint in places. It gets slippery when wet.

nl_trailer_boulders.blurb: The most visited boulder cluster at Flatrock, on the Avalon Peninsula north of St. John's, set just above the main face. Twelve problems cover a wide range: a handful of easy V0 to V2 warm-ups, a middle band around V3 to V5, and a few much harder lines, including one near the top of the scale. The blocks offer aretes, a slab, a pinchy face and a sit start from a ledge, so the style stays varied. Easy access and the short walk make it a fine place for first-time boulderers as well as experienced climbers.
nl_trailer_boulders.parking_note: In Flatrock, turn onto the public wharf just past Wade's Lane and park at the end of it.
nl_trailer_boulders.approach: Walk straight up the hill from the wharf; the trailer comes into view soon. Follow the worn path uphill from there and keep to it so no new tracks form.

nl_geometry_wall.blurb: A granite sport wall within Swift Current on the Burin Peninsula, on Newfoundland's south coast. Its eleven bolted lines are overhung and technical, with blocks, edges and cracks shaping the face. Grades begin around 5.8, but most of the routes sit in the 5.11 and 5.12 range, so it suits strong climbers more than beginners. First bolts are high and several starts are hard, so bring a stick clip. Every route finishes on rappel anchors, and the lowest-grade line is the way up to reach the tops of the others.
nl_geometry_wall.approach: Where the path ends below Tiger Wall, turn left and follow the cliff base. Beyond a large gully the trail drops steeply down to the crag.

nl_breakwater.blurb: A small coastal wall at Quidi Vidi on the edge of St. John's, in view of walkers on the breakwater across the harbour. Ten routes, mainly bolted sport lines plus one top-rope and one trad climb, run from easy 5.6 slabs to routes in the 5.12 range, with a good cluster around 5.9 and 5.10. The gentler slabs make it popular for guided days and for newer leaders. Expect rough landings; some lines want a stick clip low down, and many anchors suit top-rope setups.
nl_breakwater.approach: From Pipeline Road, walk east about 30 m, turn right onto the East Coast Trail and follow it 5 to 10 minutes to a fork, then follow the signs to a viewpoint above the base of the wall.

nl_zombie_wall.blurb: A sea cliff in the DFO (The Skerries) area just outside St. John's, with every route rising directly from the ocean. Ten climbs split evenly between sport and trad, almost all between 5.9 and 5.11 and concentrated at 5.10, so it suits climbers who are comfortable on the middle grades. The cliff is around 40 m tall, and the climbs are reached by rappelling in from trees and anchors at the top. It is the first wall you meet along the trail, and the sandstone setting feels remote despite the city being close.
